# Enums

<a id="enums-declaration"></a>

## A case with no written value counts on from the one before it, starting at zero

`rule:enums/declaration`

An enum body is a comma list of `Name` or `Name = <integer literal>`, and the optional `: int` or
`: uint` before it names the backing type ([`enums/one-backing-type`](enums.md#enums-one-backing-type)):

```
enum Status { Active, Banned }
enum Permission: uint { Read = 0b001, Write = 0b010, Admin = 0b100 }
```

The first case with no written value is `0`; every later case with no written value is the previous
case's value plus one, whether that previous value was written or counted. An explicit value resets
the counter for everything after it. A value may be negative or zero, and auto-increment continues
from a negative one.

Two cases may carry the same value. Nothing forbids the alias, because equality over an enum is
value equality and there is no identity for two names to collide on.

Two cases never carry the same name. A second case of a name the enum already declares is `E0304` at
the second one, as a class member declared twice is ([`types/declaration`](types.md#types-declaration)), and the first case
keeps its value.

<sub>See also [`enums/closed-integer-type`](enums.md#enums-closed-integer-type), [`enums/one-backing-type`](enums.md#enums-one-backing-type), [`enums/no-case-keyword`](enums.md#enums-no-case-keyword).</sub>

<a id="enums-no-case-keyword"></a>

## PHP's `case` keyword does not parse, and each one is diagnosed where it is written

`rule:enums/no-case-keyword`

There is no `case` keyword in an enum body. `case Hearts = 1;` is refused with **`E0239`**, raised
on the `case` keyword itself and naming the comma-list spelling that works
([`enums/declaration`](enums.md#enums-declaration)).

The case is *kept*: only the keyword and its `;` are consumed, so an enum written with `case` still
declares every member the rest of the program goes on to name, and one diagnostic per case is the
whole answer rather than a cascade of unresolved names behind it.

This is deliberately not `E0220` ([`enums/no-class-machinery`](enums.md#enums-no-class-machinery)). A method or a constant in an
enum body belongs somewhere else and is told so; a case belongs exactly where it is written, and
only its spelling is wrong.

<sub>See also [`enums/declaration`](enums.md#enums-declaration), [`enums/no-class-machinery`](enums.md#enums-no-class-machinery).</sub>

<a id="enums-class-scoped-enum"></a>

## An `enum` is also a member of a class or interface body, reached as `Owner::Name` and `Owner::Name::Case`, and as a bare `Name` inside its owner

`rule:enums/class-scoped-enum`

An `enum` is also a member of a class or interface body, taking no visibility modifier, reached as
`Owner::Name` and `Owner::Name::Case` from anywhere and as a bare `Name` and `Name::Case` inside its
owner's own body, and never inherited.

```nvs
namespace Shop;

final class Order {
    enum Status { Open, Paid, Cancelled }

    public Status $status = Status::Open;              // the short form, inside the owner

    public function pay(): void { $this->status = Status::Paid; }
}

final class Receipt {
    public static function label(Order::Status $s): string {   // the qualified form, anywhere
        return $s == Order::Status::Paid ? "paid" : "unpaid";
    }
}
```

Everything else about an enum holds unchanged: its body ([`enums/declaration`](enums.md#enums-declaration)), its one backing
type, its closed integer cases ([`enums/closed-integer-type`](enums.md#enums-closed-integer-type)), its zero-byte representation, and
every binding site it types ([`statements/an-enum-name-is-a-type-everywhere`](statements.md#statements-an-enum-name-is-a-type-everywhere)). The member
only changes where the declaration is written and how its name is spelled. A case is still an integer
inlined where it is written, so `Order::Status::Paid` compiles to the same constant a file-scope
`Status::Paid` does. In type position, `Order::Status::Paid` is the case's own type
([`types/enum-case-type`](types.md#types-enum-case-type)).

- **Two places, and no third.** An enum is declared at file scope or in a class or interface body. In
  an enum body it is `E0220`, whose help names the class body. In a method body, a hook, a closure or a
  block it stays `E0233` ([`classes/a-type-is-declared-at-file-scope`](classes.md#classes-a-type-is-declared-at-file-scope)). A class or an interface in
  a class body stays refused: it is one `E0233` where it is written.
- **No visibility, ever.** A modifier run in front of a body's `enum` is `E0133`. Its cases leave the
  class in every return value and every property, so a `private` enum would hide the name and not the
  values. An attribute group may stand in front of it, as in front of a file-scope enum.
- **No inheritance.** `Sub::Status`, where only an ancestor of `Sub` declares `Status`, is `E0405`
  in a type and `E0309` in a value, each naming the class that does. A subclass that inherited the name would give one enum as many names as
  its owner has descendants ([`statements/nothing-gets-a-second-name`](statements.md#statements-nothing-gets-a-second-name)).
- **Two spellings and no third.** `self::Status` and `static::Status` are `E0135` where they are
  written, as they are for a class-scoped alias ([`types/class-scoped-alias`](types.md#types-class-scoped-alias)). An enum is resolved
  before there is a receiver, so `static::` could only mean the lexical class, which the bare `Status`
  already says.
- **A name is one thing.** An owner's enum, constant and alias never share a name: the later of the
  two declarations is `E0304`.
- **No import of a member.** `use Shop\Order::Status;` is a diagnostic where it is written. A program
  imports the owner and writes `Order::Status`. A member import would give one enum a second short
  name.

**The name a program sees** is the owner's qualified name, `::`, and the member's name:
`Shop\Order::Status`. `Core\Reflect\EnumInfo::name`, a diagnostic, `nvs meta` and the error a route
capture throws all print it. `Core\Reflect\EnumInfo::of(Order::Status::class)` reads it back. The
declaration is keyed by the owner's `QName` and the member name, never by a namespace path, for the
reason [`types/class-scoped-alias`](types.md#types-class-scoped-alias) gives: `Shop\Order\Status` is also the spelling of a class
`Status` in namespace `Shop\Order`, and the two are two types with two keys.

The member exists so an enum that describes one class's state is named by its owner, as that class's
constants, aliases and methods are, and not by an owner prefix written by hand into a file-scope name
(`OrderStatus`, `InvoiceStatus`). Where an enum goes is [`enums/an-enum-lives-in-the-class-that-uses-it`](enums.md#enums-an-enum-lives-in-the-class-that-uses-it).

What it trades. Performance: nothing at run time, because a case is still an inlined integer and the
name is resolved before any code runs. Usability: a class's enums are read with it, and a name stops
carrying its owner's word. Simplicity: a second place to declare an enum and a three-part value form,
both resolved by the checker.

- **Memory:** nothing per request, because the compiled program is the one the file-scope form
  produces. At compile time it costs one enum-table entry per declaration, the same entry a
  file-scope enum pays for, and one runtime name string per enum, as before.

**Declined:**
- **Enums at file scope only.** Every program would pay for it with owner prefixes spelled by hand,
  to save one member kind in the parser.
- **`use Shop\Order::Status;`.** It gives one enum a second short name
  ([`statements/nothing-gets-a-second-name`](statements.md#statements-nothing-gets-a-second-name)), and importing the owner already costs one segment.
- **A `private` or `protected` enum.** The cases are values that leave the class, so a modifier hides
  a name and nothing else.
- **Nested classes and interfaces alongside.** A class has members, layout and dispatch of its own,
  and none of the static tables has a reading for one inside another. An enum is a closed list of
  integers and has none of that.
- **An enum in an enum body.** An enum body is a list of cases ([`enums/no-class-machinery`](enums.md#enums-no-class-machinery)), and
  a case list owning another case list says nothing a namespace does not.
- **The old file-scope `Core` names kept beside the new ones.** That is a second name for each
  enum, and there is no release that a program could have been written against.

<sub>See also [`types/class-scoped-alias`](types.md#types-class-scoped-alias), [`enums/an-enum-lives-in-the-class-that-uses-it`](enums.md#enums-an-enum-lives-in-the-class-that-uses-it), [`classes/a-type-is-declared-at-file-scope`](classes.md#classes-a-type-is-declared-at-file-scope), [`statements/nothing-gets-a-second-name`](statements.md#statements-nothing-gets-a-second-name).</sub>

<a id="enums-an-enum-lives-in-the-class-that-uses-it"></a>

## An enum one class uses is declared in that class, and an enum several classes share is declared in their namespace

`rule:enums/an-enum-lives-in-the-class-that-uses-it`

An enum exactly one class takes, returns or holds is declared in that class; an enum several classes
use, or none, is declared in their namespace. The rule binds every `Core` enum, every built-in
component's enum and every published program, and it is the default a program's own enums follow.

The test is mechanical, so two readers place one enum the same way. A class *uses* an enum when one
of its methods takes it as a parameter or returns it, or one of its properties or constants has its
type. An enum used by one class moves into it. An enum used by two or more, or only by an attribute
(`Core\Audience`, used only by `#[Access]`), stays at namespace scope. When a later member makes an
owned enum shared, the enum moves back to its namespace in the slice that adds the member.
`crates/nvs-stdlib/tests/enum_owners.rs` holds the rule for `Core`, and a reviewer's judgement does
not override it.

**A rename drops the owner's word** where the old name repeated it: `Core\Xml\NodeKind` becomes
`Core\Xml\Node::Kind`, never `Core\Xml\Node::NodeKind`. A name that does not parse as a member, because
it clashes with a keyword, keeps its old word and drops the owner's prefix the other way; the table
below says which, and today no entry needs it.

The `Core` enums that move:

| Was | Is |
|---|---|
| `Core\Order` | `Core\Arr::Order` |
| `Core\SetOn` | `Core\Arr::SetOn` |
| `Core\NormalForm` | `Core\Str::NormalForm` |
| `Core\Digest` | `Core\Hash::Digest` |
| `Core\Codec` | `Core\Compress::Codec` |
| `Core\Weekday` | `Core\Time\DateTime::Weekday` |
| `Core\Crypto\Cipher` | `Core\Crypto::Cipher` |
| `Core\Crypto\KeyFormat` | `Core\Crypto\PublicKey::Format` |
| `Core\Mime\Type` | `Core\Mime::Type` |
| `Core\Xml\NodeKind` | `Core\Xml\Node::Kind` |
| `Core\Log\Level` | `Core\Log::Level` |
| `Core\Env\Mode` | `Core\Env::Mode` |
| `Core\Response\Redirect` | `Core\Response::Redirect` |
| `Core\Response\SameSite` | `Core\Response::SameSite` |
| `Core\Cli\Stream` | `Core\Cli::Stream` |
| `Core\Cli\ColorDepth` | `Core\Cli::ColorDepth` |
| `Core\Cli\Shell` | `Core\Command::Shell` |
| `Core\Reflect\TypeKind` | `Core\Reflect::TypeKind` |
| `Core\IO\FileMode` | `Core\IO::FileMode` |
| `Core\Cldr\PluralCategory` | `Core\Cldr::PluralCategory` |
| `Core\Script\ExitReason` | `Core\Script\ExitReport::Reason` |
| `Core\Db\Tls` | `Core\Db::Tls` |
| `Core\Db\ErrorKind` | `Core\Db\DbError::Kind` |
| `Core\Db\ColumnType` | `Core\Db\Column::Type` |
| `Core\Db\Plan\Grade` | `Core\Db\Plan\Step::Grade` |
| `Core\Ldap\Scope` | `Core\Ldap\Connection::Scope` |
| `Core\Ldap\Tls` | `Core\Ldap::Tls` |
| `Core\Ldap\ErrorKind` | `Core\Ldap\LdapError::Kind` |
| `Core\Ldap\Ad\AccountType` | `Core\Ldap\Entry::AccountType` |
| `Core\Queue\State` | `Core\Queue::State` |

The `Core` enums that stay, each with the classes that share it: `Core\RoundMode` (`Math`,
`Decimal`), `Core\Charset` (`Encoding`, `IO`), `Core\Unit` (`DateTime`, `Date`, `TimeOfDay`),
`Core\Crypto\KeyKind` (four classes), `Core\Http\Method` (seven classes and `#[Route]`),
`Core\Db\Driver` (`Db`, `Db\Connection`), `Core\Db\Isolation` (`Db\Connection`,
`Db\Transaction`) and `Core\Audience` (`#[Access]` alone). A use site this table missed is placed by
the rule, and the table is corrected here. `crates/nvs-stdlib/tests/enum_owners.rs` is what decides:
a class uses an enum when a parameter, an option, a field of a settings shape, a return type or a
constant of one of its members names it.

The built-in components follow the same rule. In `Novis\Image`, every enum but `Format` moves into
`Image` (`Gravity`, `Fit`, `Filter`, `Axis`, `Blend`, `Align`, `Output`, `HashKind`,
`PlaceholderKind`), and `QrLevel` becomes `QrCode::Level`. `Format` is shared and stays. In
`Novis\Intl`, the enums become `Collator::Strength`, `Collator::CaseFirst`, `NumberFormat::Style`,
`NumberFormat::CurrencyDisplay`, `NumberFormat::CompactDisplay`, `PluralRules::Kind`,
`PluralRules::Category`, `DateFormat::Length`, `DateFormat::ZoneStyle`, `RelativeTime::Unit`,
`RelativeTime::Numeric`, `ListFormat::Type` and `Locale::Service`. `Width` is shared and stays.
A manifest names an enum's owner with its `owner` key, and the owner is the manifest's class or a
class of the component's Novis source. `crates/nvs-ext/tests/manifest.rs` decides here: a source
class uses an enum when its code names it, and the manifest's own class is not counted, because its
signatures name every enum the source classes pass through to it.

A published program — an example, an attack, a bench, a website snippet, a reference chapter's
listing — places its enums the same way. An enum two classes share stays
at file scope, and the program says so in one line where it is declared. `tests/conformance/` is the
exception: its cases pin enum behaviour at file scope and stay there.

The rule exists so a reader finds an enum where the class it describes is declared, and so the
surface is one language. A `Core` class's card and stub show its enums, and a program written against
the reference reads like the reference. An old `Core` name is gone, not deprecated: there is no
release a program could depend on, and a second spelling would be a second name
([`statements/nothing-gets-a-second-name`](statements.md#statements-nothing-gets-a-second-name)).

What it trades. Performance and memory: nothing, since placement changes a name and not a value.
Usability: every `Core` enum a program names changes spelling once, before the first release, and
`Core\Arr::sort($rows, {order: Core\Arr::Order::Desc})` reads with its class. Simplicity: one rule a
test enforces, in place of a judgement each contributor makes.

**Declined:**
- **Placement left to taste.** Two contributors would place one enum two ways, and the surface would
  drift one member at a time. A rule a test reads does not drift.
- **Every enum in a class, a shared one in whichever class came first.** The other users would name
  it through a class they do not otherwise touch, and the owner would be an accident of history.
- **Deprecated aliases for the old `Core` names.** Each is a second name for one enum, kept for
  programs that do not exist yet.
- **Moving the conformance cases too.** They pin the file-scope form, which stays a supported place
  for a shared enum, and the new form has cases of its own.

<sub>See also [`enums/class-scoped-enum`](enums.md#enums-class-scoped-enum), [`core-api/no-mode-strings`](core-api.md#core-api-no-mode-strings), [`statements/nothing-gets-a-second-name`](statements.md#statements-nothing-gets-a-second-name).</sub>

<a id="enums-closed-integer-type"></a>

## An enum declares a new, closed, named integer type

`rule:enums/closed-integer-type`

`enum Status { Active, Banned }` declares a new named integer type with a fixed set of cases, and
the enum's name is then a type like any other — a property, a parameter, a return, a local, a class
constant, an `array<T>` element, an `Iterator<T>` yield, a `foreach` binding. The `enum` keyword
appears only at the declaration site; every use site spells the enum's own name, exactly as a class
does.

A case is a compile-time constant of that type, never an object. There is no singleton to allocate,
no identity distinct from the value ([`enums/no-class-machinery`](enums.md#enums-no-class-machinery)), and no per-isolate storage
slot to build or tear down ([`enums/representation`](enums.md#enums-representation)).

The set is closed, and closed means checked: a value no case names never becomes a case by default
or by silent coercion. `EnumName` is its own kind of type atom rather than a class reference, so a
name that resolves to an enum is not a class name and is never treated as one.

A closed set of named values is checked at the same boundary as any other typed input: untrusted
input becomes a case only through the one throwing `as` every other conversion uses
([`types/conversion`](types.md#types-conversion)), so there is no second per-enum API for a reviewer or an analyzer to know
about.

**Declined:**
- **A case as a singleton object, with methods and interfaces.** It allocates a case and carries
  identity, methods and interfaces for something an integer and a `match` already do
  ([`enums/no-class-machinery`](enums.md#enums-no-class-machinery)).
- **Singleton case objects with no methods and no interfaces.** That keeps the allocation and drops
  the only features that would pay for it.
- **A conversion into an enum that always succeeds.** Turning any integer into an enum value, even one
  no case names, is the silent coercion `as` never performs; a value no case names throws.

<sub>See also [`enums/declaration`](enums.md#enums-declaration), [`enums/one-backing-type`](enums.md#enums-one-backing-type), [`enums/no-class-machinery`](enums.md#enums-no-class-machinery), [`enums/representation`](enums.md#enums-representation).</sub>

<a id="enums-one-backing-type"></a>

## Every enum is backed by exactly one integer type, and nothing else backs one

`rule:enums/one-backing-type`

`enum E: int` and `enum E: uint` name the backing type; with no `: T` written it is `int`. Nothing
else backs an enum — `enum E: string` is refused with **`E0219`**, and so is a case whose value is
not an integer literal.

That is the only shape. There is no *pure* enum: the "no backing value"
declaration is the auto-incrementing default nobody overrode ([`enums/declaration`](enums.md#enums-declaration)), and a
program that only ever compares cases never has to look at the integer. There is no `string`
backing: a string-valued case would be a heap-allocated, interned buffer where a scalar fits the
value's existing payload for nothing ([`enums/representation`](enums.md#enums-representation)).

The two backings are told apart everywhere the type is. A `uint`-backed case converts with `as uint`
only, an `int`-backed one with `as int` only, and each refuses the other.

<sub>See also [`enums/declaration`](enums.md#enums-declaration), [`enums/closed-integer-type`](enums.md#enums-closed-integer-type), [`enums/representation`](enums.md#enums-representation).</sub>

<a id="enums-representation"></a>

## An enum value costs nothing beyond the integer it is

`rule:enums/representation`

An enum value is its backing integer and nothing more — zero additional bytes over what `int` or
`uint` already costs, no allocation, no refcount, no descriptor. Where the static type is known,
which the type system makes the common case, codegen already knows which enum it is and there is
nothing further to carry.

Materialized into a tagged value — a `mixed`, an `array<mixed>` element, an erased parameter — a
case takes an **enum tag of its own**, one per backing type: `EnumInt` over an `int` payload and
`EnumUint` over a `uint` one. A condition, a type test, an anonymous function parameter's check and a declared
slot's write check read that tag, so a case in a `mixed` is always truthy ([`enums/truthiness`](enums.md#enums-truthiness)),
`is int` is `false` for it and `is` an enum is `false` for a plain integer. Every reader that only
decodes the value — printing, conversion and the `==` comparison — reads it as its backing integer. The tag
names no enum, so two enums with the same backing are not told apart in a `mixed`. `Core\Serialize`
writes a case as a node kind of its own over the same payload, so a case read back from it, from
`Core\Cache`, from a session, from a topic or from a placed task is still a case.

One tag per backing keeps the payload's signedness with the value, so nothing reads a `uint` case above
`i64::MAX` as a negative number, and no padding byte is written. The tag is written only where a case
is materialized into a tagged value, so a statically typed enum still costs nothing. An anonymous
function's enum parameter accepts a case of an enum with its backing and throws `LogicError` for an
`int`, and an `int` or `float` parameter throws for a case. An `array<T>` element-tag walk reads the
enum tag too. The `==` comparison and the hash beside it read the backing integer, so a case in a
`mixed` is equal there to an integer of the same value, and the two agree. `$any as Rank` still converts an
integer to a case, because the conversion reads the payload, and `Core\Reflect`'s type kind reports a
case in a `mixed` as `int` or `uint`.

Crossing an isolate boundary copies a plain scalar, with no object identity to preserve or discard.

- **Memory:** an enum value costs exactly what its `int` or `uint` costs, in the same payload. Nothing
  is held per enum, per request or per isolate: no case table, no singleton and no type descriptor.

**Declined:**
- **A case keeping the `Int` or `Uint` tag in a `mixed`.** A case backed by `0` would then be falsy
  there and truthy where its type is known, `is int` would be `true` for it, and `is Rank` would be
  `true` for any integer equal to one of its cases.
- **One enum tag with the signedness in a padding byte.** Every tag write would have to write the pad,
  and every reader would need a second byte to read the payload.
- **The enum's identity in the padding bytes.** It tells two enums apart in a `mixed`, which no rule
  asks for, and it costs a store on every materialization.
- **The payload-reading tag accessor returning the enum tags.** Every reader that decodes a payload
  would need a new arm, a few hundred of them, for a value they all read as its integer.

<sub>See also [`enums/no-class-machinery`](enums.md#enums-no-class-machinery), [`enums/one-backing-type`](enums.md#enums-one-backing-type), [`enums/closed-integer-type`](enums.md#enums-closed-integer-type).</sub>

<a id="enums-truthiness"></a>

## An enum case is always truthy, whatever integer backs it

`rule:enums/truthiness`

An enum case in a condition is **always truthy**, whatever integer backs it. `Signal::Idle` backed
by `0` is truthy; so is a case backed by a negative value.

An enum follows the object row of the truthy table rather than the integer row its backing type
might suggest ([`enums/representation`](enums.md#enums-representation)). A case is a value of its own type, not a number, and
judging it by its backing integer would make the branch `if ($status)` takes depend on which integer
a declaration happened to give the case. It also keeps every ported condition meaning what it
meant: a PHP enum case is an object, a PHP object is never falsy, so `if ($status)` over a case has
only ever been true.

Lowering reads this statically: a condition whose static type is an enum needs no truthiness helper
and no comparison at all.

<sub>See also [`enums/representation`](enums.md#enums-representation), [`enums/no-class-machinery`](enums.md#enums-no-class-machinery), [`enums/closed-integer-type`](enums.md#enums-closed-integer-type).</sub>

<a id="enums-no-class-machinery"></a>

## A case is an integer constant, and an enum body declares nothing but cases

`rule:enums/no-class-machinery`

`EnumName::CaseName` **is** an integer constant, inlined at every use site the way a literal `5` is:
nothing is allocated, nothing is refcounted, there is no descriptor, and there is no per-isolate
storage slot for an enum at all ([`enums/representation`](enums.md#enums-representation)).

An enum body therefore declares only cases and an optional backing type. An `implements` clause is
refused with **`E0218`**; a method, a property, a class constant or a trait use inside the body is
refused with **`E0220`**, which names the class such a member belongs on instead. A case has no
members of its own, and is not an array key — index with `$case as int`.

An enum has no constructor. `new E()` and the constructor reference `E::constructor` are each
**`E0870`** at the enum's name, whose help says a case is written `E::Case`. A user attribute on an
enum or an enum case is `E0871` ([`attributes/attach-sites-and-forms`](attributes.md#attributes-attach-sites-and-forms)).

What a program writes for each job:

| Job | Novis |
|---|---|
| a case's integer | `E::A as int` (or `as uint`) |
| a case from an integer | `$n as E` / `$n as ?E` |
| a case's name | a `match` of your own |
| every case | a `static` method of your own returning `array<E>` |
| methods, constants, an interface | a class that takes the enum |

Behaviour over an enum lives on some other class as a `static` method taking the enum, because there
is no standalone-function destination for it to go to ([`classes/no-free-functions-or-constants`](classes.md#classes-no-free-functions-or-constants)).

A case that is a constant is free to inline. A case that is a heap reference is inlined only once the
optimiser has proved it immutable.

**Declined:**
- **`::from()` and `::tryFrom()`.** Building a case from its integer is the checked `as`, one
  conversion operator rather than a second API on every enum ([`types/conversion`](types.md#types-conversion)).
- **`->value` and `->name`.** The integer is `as int`, and the name is a `match` or
  [`enums/reflection`](enums.md#enums-reflection).
- **A flags enum with `| & ^ ~` on the enum type itself.** Bitwise operators apply to the backing
  integer only ([`types/arithmetic`](types.md#types-arithmetic)), so flags are combined after `as uint` and converted back
  with the checked `as`.
- **Static methods on a class that the checker treats as belonging to the enum.** It is dedicated
  syntax for what a `static` method taking the enum already does.

<sub>See also [`enums/closed-integer-type`](enums.md#enums-closed-integer-type), [`enums/representation`](enums.md#enums-representation), [`enums/no-case-keyword`](enums.md#enums-no-case-keyword), [`enums/reflection`](enums.md#enums-reflection).</sub>

<a id="enums-reflection"></a>

## Reflection describes an enum's shape and grants it nothing a class has

`rule:enums/reflection`

`Core\Reflect\EnumInfo::of(Status::class)` reports an enum's shape as ordinary structural metadata —
the type's name and its closed case list — the same way `ClassInfo` reports a class's shape.

The name is the one a program writes to reach the enum from anywhere. For a file-scope enum it is the
qualified name, `Shop\Status`. For an enum declared in a class or interface body it is the owner's
qualified name, `::` and the member's name, `Shop\Order::Status` ([`enums/class-scoped-enum`](enums.md#enums-class-scoped-enum)), and
`EnumInfo::of(Order::Status::class)` finds it by that name. A diagnostic, `nvs meta` and the
error a route capture throws print the same string, so one enum has one printed name everywhere.

It grants an enum nothing it does not already have: no method dispatch, no interface, no case
identity, and nothing that acts on a value. It is a second description of the same closed integer
type ([`enums/closed-integer-type`](enums.md#enums-closed-integer-type)), not a reopening of [`enums/no-class-machinery`](enums.md#enums-no-class-machinery) — a
description of a case list is not a `::cases()` the language does not have.

<sub>See also [`enums/no-class-machinery`](enums.md#enums-no-class-machinery), [`enums/closed-integer-type`](enums.md#enums-closed-integer-type).</sub>
